routes.description: Establish that God is required to ground objective moral value and duty and to provide the ultimate significance and accountability that complete an objective moral framework.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if intrinsic value is grounded in God's nature, categorical duty in divine commands rather than convention, and the lasting significance and accountability of moral action in a theistic order.

motionBridge.description: Show that objective values, duties, human significance, and accountability jointly require God.

centralBridges.description: Ground intrinsic human worth and objective goodness in God's nature while explaining why naturalistic capacities or evolutionary origins are insufficient.
Ground categorical moral obligations in divine commands and distinguish genuine duties from social conditioning, agreement, or convention.
Explain why enduring moral significance and ultimate accountability require consequences beyond extinction and temporal human affairs.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how divine accountability reconciles moral obligation with prudential reasons and supports responsible moral agency.
Distinguish fallible moral knowledge from objective truth and preserve transcultural criticism of conduct and institutions.

routes.description: Establish that stance-independent moral reasons, objective duties, human significance, and responsibility can be explained within secular moral realism without a divine ground or eternal consequences.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if secular accounts supply objective moral standards and categorical reasons, explain responsible agency and moral criticism, and show that finite harms, benefits, relationships, and actions retain real significance without cosmic permanence.

motionBridge.description: Show that secular moral realism can adequately ground every objective moral domain placed in dispute without requiring God.

centralBridges.description: Explain objective morality through desire-independent categorical reasons, substantive harm-and-help standards, or basic moral facts.
Explain moral requirements through decisive reasons or fair rational agreement without presupposing a personal lawgiver.
Ground genuine human significance in the objective importance of finite lives, harms, relationships, and actions rather than eternal cosmic effects.
Ground responsibility in rational agency and defend the authority of moral reasons even when morality conflicts with prudential self-interest.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain disagreement and historical moral error as compatible with objective truth and corrigible through reflective reasoning.
Demonstrate how secular principles yield determinate judgments about atrocities, innocent victims, and harms to sentient animals.

sections.title: Objective Value and Intrinsic Human Worth
sections.rationale: The motion requires an account of what makes value stance-independent and whether human worth is grounded by God, rational capacities, harm, or irreducible moral facts.

sections.title: Moral Duty, Categorical Reasons, and Lawgiving
sections.rationale: The principal grounding clash concerns whether genuine obligation needs divine command or can arise from objective reasons, rational agreement, and mutual moral authority.

sections.title: Rational Agency and Naturalistic Grounding
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether reflective capacities can explain moral responsibility and wrongness, or merely identify valuable features whose objective status still requires a deeper ground.

sections.title: Finite Life, Extinction, and Moral Significance
sections.rationale: The competing routes must establish whether actions and relationships need eternal consequences to matter objectively or possess genuine importance within finite human lives.

sections.title: Accountability, Salvation, and Prudential Conflict
sections.rationale: The accountability burden includes ultimate justice, the relation between morality and self-interest, and whether the proposed theistic mechanism consistently delivers deserved consequences.

sections.title: Moral Knowledge, Progress, and Practical Application
sections.rationale: Disagreement, historical error, atrocities, and treatment of animals test whether each foundation supports reliable moral criticism and substantive guidance without conflating access with truth.

moves.speaker: Shelly Kagan
moves.proposition: Right and wrong can be grounded in whether conduct harms people or unjustifiably fails to help them.
moves.attributionBasis: Kagan explicitly introduces this passage as his own illustrative outline of a plausible secular ethical theory.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies a substantive secular criterion linking wrongness to harming people and unjustified failures to help.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly develops a central secular standard, though the relevant circumstances remain compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The harm-and-help criterion is recoverable, but the scope of relevant failures to help is left implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: It is presented as a plausible illustrative secular theory rather than as a uniquely demonstrated account.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from harms and failures to help to rightness and wrongness is coherent but leaves justificatory exceptions underexplained.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Ordinary moral examples support the criterion, but the warrant making harm objectively reason-giving is substantially compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies one of the principal substantive standards for the central objective-reasons bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move develops its own criterion and does not materially depend on interpreting an opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt defines wrong action through hurting people or failing to help in relevant circumstances and right action through restraint and aid.

moves.speaker: Shelly Kagan
moves.proposition: Objective moral facts consist in overriding categorical reasons that do not depend on anyone's opinions, desires, or goals.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage continues Kagan's uninterrupted opening case and repeatedly states his account in explicit first-person terms.

response.rationale: This constructive move expressly defines objective morality as universal, desire-independent, overriding categorical reasons.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it states the secular realist account in unusually direct and burden-specific terms.

precisionFindings.rationale: Categorical reasons, their independence from desires, and their overriding role are stated consistently and recoverably.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The definitional claim is clear, but the excerpt does not fully defend why such reasons exist or always override.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The account consistently connects objectivity to desire-independent categorical reasons, with the existence warrant remaining implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual explanation is specific, but the overriding authority of the proposed reasons is asserted more than independently defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It nearly defines the completion condition for the secular objective-reasons bridge and directly advances that burden.

representationalCharity.rationale: The passage primarily articulates its positive account rather than characterizing a live opposing interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says everyone has reasons independent of particular desires or goals and calls those reasons overriding and categorical.

moves.speaker: Shelly Kagan
moves.proposition: Objective moral rules can be grounded in those that perfectly rational agents would agree to behind a veil of ignorance.
moves.attributionBasis: Kagan introduces contractarianism by name and develops its bargaining procedure, objectivity, and necessity in one sustained passage.

response.rationale: This constructive move offers rational agreement behind a veil of ignorance as a secular source of objective moral rules.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it gives a recognizable procedure and source for duty, though crucial bargaining constraints remain compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contract procedure is clear, but what perfect rationality and the veil require is only partly specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The account is offered as one possible deeper secular story, with its illustrative rather than conclusive status apparent.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The procedure coherently links fair rational choice to rules, but the bridge from hypothetical agreement to categorical obligation is compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The veil and rational-bargainer device provide structure, while the authority and determinacy of its outcome receive limited defense.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly addresses the central secular-duty requirement by proposing a nondivine source of governing moral rules.

representationalCharity.rationale: The passage constructs a contractarian account without materially relying on a disputed portrayal of its opponent.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says moral rules are those perfectly rational agents would give themselves while reasoning without knowledge of their identities.

moves.speaker: Shelly Kagan
moves.proposition: Moral requirements need no personal lawgiver, just as the requirement of non-contradiction needs no cosmic logician.
moves.attributionBasis: Kagan states the lawgiver objection, tests it through an extended analogy, and explicitly gives his skeptical conclusion.

response.rationale: This constructive move directly argues that genuine requirements need not originate in a person, using non-contradiction as the analogy.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly addresses the personal-lawgiver issue, although the analogy's relevant similarity is not fully defended.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between personified talk of laws and an actual personal lawgiver is explicit and consistently applied.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The analogy makes the conclusion plausible, but logical and moral requirements may differ in authority or action-guidance.

charity.alternative: Moral obligations differ from logical constraints because obligations characteristically address agents and may require authoritative prescription.
charity.decisiveQualification: The analogy establishes that some requirements lack personal authors, not by itself that categorical moral duties do.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The analogy supports the possibility of impersonal requirements, but the transfer from logic to moral obligation leaves a material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The non-contradiction analogy is concrete and relevant, though no independent account of moral normativity completes the comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the claimed need for a personal lawgiver at the heart of the central secular-duty dispute.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move engages the personal-lawgiver intuition fairly but omits a developed comparison between logical necessity and moral authority.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes personified talk about reason from an actual author of non-contradiction and applies that distinction to moral requirements.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: God's holy and loving nature supplies an objective standard of value, while naturalism leaves human worth dependent on contingent evolutionary adaptations.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig labels this his first claim and develops it continuously through divine-nature grounding and a naturalistic evolutionary contrast.

components.text: Explain what makes purportedly objective moral reasons and human worth objectively valuable rather than merely asserted.
Explain why persons who can be harmed or helped possess objective moral worth under naturalism.

response.rationale: The move contacts both secular value claims by supplying a divine-nature standard and challenging naturalism's explanation of human worth, though it does not separately refute categorical reasons.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive grounding demand but leaves the secular basic-reasons alternative insufficiently compared.

precisionFindings.rationale: Divine nature is identified as the standard, but the scope of the claim that naturalism leaves no basis is broad and qualified only implicitly.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The positive proposal is intelligible, but the move overstates the failure of naturalistic alternatives without a serious rival comparison.

charity.alternative: Secular realism may treat worth or categorical reasons as basic rather than as products of evolutionary adaptation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Evolutionary origins of belief do not alone show that the represented values are contingent or unreal.

logicalCoherence.rationale: God's nature can function as a proposed standard, but the inference from naturalistic evolution to absent objective worth leaves a material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The divine attributes and evolutionary contrast are asserted clearly, but the exclusion of secular basic value receives little supporting comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central theistic objective-value bridge by proposing a ground and challenging naturalistic worth.

representationalCharity.rationale: The evolutionary contrast materially compresses the strongest secular realist alternative and its ontology-belief distinction.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies God's holy and loving nature as an absolute standard and asks what basis for human moral worth remains without God.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Objective moral duties require commands flowing from God's moral nature because social conditioning and social contracts yield conventions rather than genuine obligations.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly marks this as his second argument and contrasts divine commands with the secular social-contract account attributed to Kagan.

components.text: Show why rational social agreement yields genuine categorical obligations rather than revisable human conventions.
Show why genuine moral duties require authoritative personal commands rather than impersonal normative requirements.

response.rationale: The move directly contrasts divine commands with contract and conditioning, but largely asserts rather than demonstrates why impersonal requirements cannot obligate.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts both central demands but does not resolve the logic analogy or hypothetical-contract authority in detail.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between divine commands and convention is stable, while the necessity of a commander remains an implicit premise.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that objective duties require divine commands exceeds the supplied argument against impersonal or contractarian normativity.

charity.alternative: A secular account can distinguish ideal rational agreement or categorical reasons from actual social conditioning and convention.
charity.decisiveQualification: Calling contracts conventional does not answer the idealized rational-authority account actually proposed.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Commands flowing from a moral nature avoid simple arbitrariness, but the necessity of commands and dismissal of secular duty remain underargued.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move gives a definite theological mechanism but relies substantially on assertion when excluding impersonal and contractarian obligations.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central theistic duty bridge and attacks the principal secular account of obligation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes the contract view but materially weakens it by assimilating ideal rational agreement to ordinary convention.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt defines objective obligation, roots duties in divine commands flowing from God's nature, and contrasts them with secular convention.

moves.speaker: Shelly Kagan
moves.proposition: Moral responsibility applies to rational agents because they can reflect on reasons and regulate their behavior, unlike animals or very young children.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator-free exchange clearly shifts from Craig's challenge to Kagan's extended first-person answer and examples.

components.text: Explain what distinguishes morally responsible human agents from nonreflective animals on a naturalistic account.

response.rationale: The move answers the agency challenge by identifying reflective recognition of reasons, although it does not independently ground the objective value of those reasons.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it directly contacts the responsibility distinction but leaves the deeper objective-grounding component unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The relevant class is explicitly limited to agents capable of reflecting on conduct and recognizing reasons.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The comparative claim about reflective agents is proportionate to the examples and does not purport to settle all grounding questions.

charity.alternative: The theistic challenge concerns objective value, not merely the psychological capacity to reflect on reasons.
charity.decisiveQualification: Reflective capacity explains responsibility conditions but not by itself why the recognized reasons are objectively authoritative.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The contrast between reflective agents and nonreflective animals coherently explains differential responsibility with one bounded grounding gap.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The animal and human comparison supplies relevant support, though the relation between reflection and full responsibility is compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies a major component of the central secular responsibility-and-accountability bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response fairly addresses the agency component, though it does not fully preserve the opponent's deeper grounding demand.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts lions unable to reflect with humans who can recognize reasons and regulate conduct in light of them.

moves.speaker: Shelly Kagan
moves.proposition: Once agents can step back from conduct, assess standards, and recognize reasons against harm, no additional supernatural ingredient is required for wrongness.
moves.attributionBasis: Kagan explicitly restates Craig's revised question and answers it continuously in the first person throughout the window.

components.text: Explain whether naturalistic reflective capacities require an additional supernatural ingredient for moral wrongness.

response.rationale: The move directly denies the need for a further supernatural ingredient once reflective assessment and reason recognition are present, but treats objective authority as already available.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the supernatural-ingredient demand while compressing the distinct question of why standards bind objectively.

precisionFindings.rationale: The capacity threshold is clear, but what counts as standards agents are prepared to endorse is not fully stabilized.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that no more machinery is needed slightly outruns the explanation of objective reasons and endorsement-independent authority.

charity.alternative: The opponent may accept reflective capacity while asking what makes its objects or possessors objectively valuable.
charity.decisiveQualification: Having machinery for reflection does not alone settle the metaphysical grounding of the reasons assessed.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Reflection can explain responsiveness to reasons, but the move leaves a material bridge from endorsement-capacity to objective wrongness.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The evolutionary capacity story is concrete, while its sufficiency for normativity is asserted without developed rival comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially advances the central secular responsibility bridge by identifying the capacities needed for reason-guided agency.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response recognizes the natural-versus-supernatural challenge but only partially preserves its separate value-grounding component.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says that once creatures can step back, assess conduct against standards, and recognize reasons, the relevant machinery is in place.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Identifying distinctive human capacities such as reflection, love, creativity, and communication does not yet explain why those capacities or their possessors are objectively valuable under naturalism.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig refers to Kagan's book and frames the passage as his own challenge concerning explanatory grounding under naturalism.

components.text: Explain why reflective capacities and the persons possessing them have objective value rather than merely being identifiable natural features.
Distinguish explaining responsible capacities from explaining the objective authority and value attached to those capacities.

response.rationale: The move directly exposes the explanatory gap between identifying capacities and grounding their value, though it offers no further positive defense of divine grounding here.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it explicitly contacts the decisive sufficiency inference and states the remaining explanatory demand.

precisionFindings.rationale: The challenge carefully distinguishes identifying valuable capacities from explaining why they are objectively valuable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move frames a focused explanatory challenge rather than claiming that no secular answer could possibly be supplied.

charity.alternative: A secular realist may regard persons or their capacities as intrinsically valuable basic facts requiring no deeper explanation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Explanatory stopping points may be legitimate, although consistency requires explaining why this is not premature.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between locating value-bearing properties and grounding their value is clear and directly exposes an explanatory gap.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The challenge is textually specific and invokes a relevant explanatory principle, with the legitimacy of further regress left open.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central secular objective-reasons bridge and supports the corresponding theistic value-grounding requirement.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly acknowledges the intrinsic-value stopping point and challenges its explanatory adequacy without caricaturing it.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks whether treating persons and distinctive capacities as intrinsically valuable cuts off the search for explanation too soon.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: If naturalism ends in universal extinction with no ultimate accountability, moral choices lack enduring significance because every outcome leaves the final universe neither better nor worse.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig answers Kagan's direct question and develops his familiar heat-death and accountability argument in a continuous response.

components.text: Explain why finite harms and benefits cease to matter objectively merely because the universe eventually reaches extinction.
Show why desire-independent moral reasons require enduring cosmic consequences or postmortem accountability.

response.rationale: The move supplies issue-bearing claims about extinction and accountability but does not answer why temporally finite harms or categorical reasons cannot retain objective significance.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it squarely raises cosmic permanence but leaves the decisive finite-value inference unsupported.

precisionFindings.rationale: Enduring or ultimate significance is sometimes treated as equivalent to significance without explicitly defending that scope restriction.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The heat-death premise is relevant, but the conclusion that present choices lack significance is much stronger than the supplied warrant.

charity.alternative: Finite events can possess objective local value even if they do not alter the universe's final physical state.
charity.decisiveQualification: Lack of eternal effects does not logically entail lack of value while the affected lives and relationships exist.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument moves from identical final cosmic states to absent moral significance without defending the crucial permanence-to-value conditional.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The extinction scenario is specific, but it supports only impermanence, not the stronger conclusion that finite outcomes lack objective importance.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central theistic significance-and-accountability bridge despite its underdefended inference.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes finite outcomes but materially discounts the strongest local-value interpretation by equating ultimate and genuine significance.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes a future of dead stars, no accountability, and an unchanged final universe to question the significance of moral choices.

moves.speaker: Shelly Kagan
moves.proposition: Torture matters objectively to victims, families, and communities even if it never changes the universe's eternal endpoint.
moves.attributionBasis: Kagan directly challenges Craig's heat-death response, using Craig's torture example and repeatedly distinguishing local importance from cosmic permanence.

components.text: Identify why identical eventual cosmic outcomes do not entail that present torture and its effects lack objective significance.

response.rationale: The move expressly identifies the invalid slide from no eternal cosmic difference to no present importance and states that suffering matters to victims and communities.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it explicitly attacks the decisive inference and supplies a concrete defeating counterexample.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between cosmic permanence and importance to affected finite beings is explicit and consistently maintained.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The counterexample warrants rejection of the claimed entailment without purporting to prove a complete secular value theory.

charity.alternative: The opponent may mean ultimate cosmic significance rather than all present importance.
charity.decisiveQualification: That narrower claim does not establish the disputed conclusion that finite actions lack objective moral significance.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The torture counterexample clearly defeats the inference from no eternal effect to no morally important effect on finite persons.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Victims, families, and communities provide specific representative bearers of harm, with only the deeper value ontology left unstated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the central finite-significance bridge by defending the objective importance of finite suffering.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response isolates the narrower defensible claim and accurately explains why it fails to establish the stronger conclusion.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt insists that torture matters to victims regardless of cosmic permanence and distinguishes human importance from the universe's endpoint.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: On atheism prudential self-interest can conflict with moral duty, whereas divine accountability ultimately reconciles prudent action with morally required sacrifice.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly clarifies his third argument, contrasts atheism with theism, and confirms Kagan's summary of his proposed reconciliation.

components.text: Show why moral reasons cannot rationally outweigh conflicting prudential self-interest on a secular account.
Explain why reflective agents cannot act rationally on moral reasons when doing so conflicts with self-interest.

response.rationale: The move proposes divine accountability as a harmonizing mechanism but does not establish its asserted premise that prudence otherwise trumps morality.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it identifies the conflict but leaves the decisive comparative-weight question unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: Prudence, rationality, and self-interest are treated as aligned without clarifying whether prudence necessarily has overriding force.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that prudence would trump morality is asserted without a warrant ranking prudential reasons above categorical moral reasons.

charity.alternative: Secular rationality may include moral reasons strong enough to override self-interested prudential reasons.
charity.decisiveQualification: A conflict between reason types does not establish which reason has greater rational weight.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Divine consequences can align incentives, but the inference that secular prudence rationally trumps morality is an unsupported conditional.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conflict is intelligible, while both the prudential ranking and the promised accountability mechanism are substantially asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary theistic prudence-and-agency bridge, near the upper end of that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move materially weakens the secular alternative by assuming rather than addressing the possible priority of moral reasons.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says atheistic prudence and morality can conflict, assumes self-interest prevails, and contrasts this with theistic accountability.

moves.speaker: Shelly Kagan
moves.proposition: Conflict between morality and prudence does not establish that self-interest prevails, because moral reasons may carry greater rational weight.
moves.attributionBasis: Kagan rejects Craig's characterization of his view and then formulates a direct question about why moral reasons cannot outweigh prudential ones.

components.text: Identify why conflict between morality and prudence does not establish that prudential self-interest rationally trumps morality.

response.rationale: The move expressly isolates the unsupported ranking inference and proposes that moral reasons may instead carry the greater rational weight.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it explicitly contacts and defeats the decisive inference rather than merely restating secular disagreement.

precisionFindings.rationale: The response precisely distinguishes existence of conflict from the separate ranking of moral and prudential reasons.

calibrationFindings.rationale: It only claims that moral reasons may outweigh prudence, which is sufficient to defeat the opponent's unsupported necessity claim.

charity.alternative: The theistic argument may concern incentive harmony rather than the intrinsic rational weight of moral reasons.
charity.decisiveQualification: Incentive harmony can be useful without proving that morality is irrational or nonauthoritative when harmony is absent.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between conflict and priority is explicit, and the counterpossibility directly blocks the opponent's inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual rebuttal needs no extensive empirical evidence, though a full theory ranking reasons is not supplied.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the subsidiary theistic prudence bridge and reaches the top of the subsidiary range.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response preserves the plausible harmony claim while accurately rejecting the stronger rational-priority conclusion.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt accepts that morality and prudence may conflict but rejects the inference that only self-interested action is rational.

moves.speaker: Shelly Kagan
moves.proposition: Fair rational agreement condemns Nazi killing objectively because perfectly rational bargainers behind appropriate constraints would prohibit killing innocent people.
moves.attributionBasis: Kagan gives an uninterrupted answer to an audience question about whether victorious Nazis could determine morality by controlling society.

components.text: Show that ideal rational agreement can generate objective condemnation rather than merely report prevailing social convention.

response.rationale: The move distinguishes actual Nazi acceptance from ideal rational agreement and states the latter would prohibit killing innocents, directly contacting the convention objection.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it contacts the decisive convention issue but compresses the argument for the bargainers' determinate prohibition.

precisionFindings.rationale: Actual belief and ideal contract terms are explicitly separated, and the relevant prohibition is clearly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The anticipated prohibition is plausible, but the speaker acknowledges that the supporting contract argument would require more time.

charity.alternative: The divine-lawgiver objection is that hypothetical agreement still lacks genuine authority even if its verdict is attractive.
charity.decisiveQualification: Correctly predicting condemnation does not by itself establish the contract's categorical binding force.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction from actual convention is sound, but the conclusion about ideal bargainers and categorical authority retains a material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Nazi case is specific, while the crucial derivation of the innocent-killing prohibition is expressly deferred.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly demonstrates practical application of secular contract principles at the top of the subsidiary tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response fairly answers the relativism concern but leaves the stronger authority objection substantially unresolved.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says Nazi opinion is irrelevant and predicts that perfectly rational bargainers would prohibit killing innocent people.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Recognizing religious atrocities as wrong supports objective moral criticism, while such criticism requires a transcendent standard rather than the mere fact that a person believes in God.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig answers an audience question in the first person, gives several religious examples, and explicitly distinguishes moral belief from moral grounding.

components.text: Show why the secular contract criterion cannot objectively condemn atrocities without a transcendent divine standard.
Explain why categorical reasons cannot support transcultural criticism unless grounded in God.

response.rationale: The move correctly distinguishes moral belief from grounding and asserts a transcendent standard, but it does not answer how the secular criteria fail to condemn atrocities.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it addresses the same issue yet leaves the decisive insufficiency claim unsupported.

precisionFindings.rationale: The belief-grounding distinction is precise, but 'transcendent' is not sufficiently specified to exclude secular stance-independent facts.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Examples support objective criticism but do not establish that only a divine transcendent standard can ground it.

charity.alternative: Secular categorical reasons or ideal rational agreement may provide stance-independent standards for condemning atrocities.
charity.decisiveQualification: Agreement that atrocities are objectively wrong does not decide whether their ground must be personal or divine.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The epistemology-grounding distinction is sound, but the inference from objective criticism to a divine standard is underdetermined.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Religious atrocities are relevant examples, while the exclusive necessity of divine grounding receives little comparative support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary theistic transcultural-criticism bridge, though not its central value ground at full strength.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move acknowledges the opponent's moral verdict but materially omits its proposed secular grounding mechanisms.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites recognized religious wrongs, distinguishes believing in God from moral conduct, and asserts the need for a transcendent standard.

moves.speaker: Shelly Kagan
moves.proposition: Christian salvation through Christ appears to conflict with moral accountability because an evildoer may escape deserved punishment through repentance.
moves.attributionBasis: The question explicitly contrasts salvation through Jesus with Craig's preceding account of accountability and is followed by Craig's direct answer.

components.text: Explain how salvation through repentance remains consistent with the claim that evildoers receive deserved accountability.

response.rationale: The move directly identifies a potential internal tension between promised ultimate accountability and salvation that may release an evildoer from deserved punishment.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, the concise challenge explicitly contacts the accountability mechanism and states the apparent contradiction.

precisionFindings.rationale: The challenge is explicitly framed as an apparent tension and clearly identifies the two Christian claims at issue.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker says the doctrines appear difficult to reconcile rather than claiming a demonstrated contradiction.

charity.alternative: Christian doctrine may preserve punishment through substitutionary atonement rather than simply canceling deserved consequences.
charity.decisiveQualification: Unless that mechanism is supplied, repentance appears to separate personal wrongdoing from the threatened punishment.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The prima facie tension follows clearly from the stated interpretation of accountability and salvation, subject to a possible doctrinal answer.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The two propositions are specifically juxtaposed, though the challenge depends on a simplified account of Christian atonement.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central theistic significance-and-accountability bridge by testing its internal consistency.

representationalCharity.rationale: The challenge is cautiously framed and leaves room for a reconciliation while identifying the precise missing mechanism.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts punishment and reward accountability with salvation through Jesus and cautiously states that the two appear in tension.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Christian salvation preserves divine justice because Christ bears the deserved penalty for sin, allowing repentant sinners to receive grace without eliminating accountability.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig expressly introduces the Christian view and gives a continuous theological answer to Kagan's immediately preceding salvation challenge.

components.text: Explain how forgiveness of a repentant wrongdoer can preserve punishment and divine justice rather than eliminate accountability.

response.rationale: The move directly supplies substitutionary punishment as the reconciliation: the penalty is borne by Christ while the repentant sinner receives grace.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it explicitly contacts the tension and provides the missing doctrinal mechanism, though moral objections to substitution remain.

precisionFindings.rationale: Penalty, divine justice, substitution, deserved punishment, and grace are distinguished clearly enough to recover the answer.

calibrationFindings.rationale: As an account of internal Christian consistency, the response states the relevant doctrine directly and fits its explanatory aim.

charity.alternative: Accountability may require that the wrongdoer personally bear deserved punishment rather than transfer it to an innocent substitute.
charity.decisiveQualification: Substitution preserves payment of a penalty but does not automatically establish personal desert or fairness of transfer.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Substitution provides an internally intelligible reconciliation, though the justice of transferring punishment leaves a material normative bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The mechanism is clearly specified, but its fairness and the claim that it fully preserves accountability are not independently defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central theistic accountability bridge by explaining how salvation is claimed to preserve justice.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response accurately meets the stated doctrinal tension but omits the strongest moral qualification concerning transferred punishment.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says Christ bears the penalty demanded by divine justice so that sinners may receive grace without the penalty going unpaid.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Cultural disagreement reflects fallible and selfish human access to moral truth rather than the absence of objective values, and a transcendent standard permits criticism of corrupt societies.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig distinguishes moral epistemology from ontology in his characteristic framework and then invokes a transcendent standard against sociocultural relativism.

response.rationale: This constructive move separates fallible moral knowledge from objective moral reality and invokes a standard for criticizing corrupt societies.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly answers an important epistemic objection, though the divine necessity of the standard is not established here.

precisionFindings.rationale: The epistemology-ontology distinction and the fallibility qualification are explicit, stable, and consistently applied.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move appropriately claims compatibility between error and objectivity rather than treating disagreement as positive proof of theism.

charity.alternative: A secular realist can also distinguish moral truth from fallible access and criticize societies by stance-independent reasons.
charity.decisiveQualification: The epistemic distinction answers relativism but does not uniquely support a divine transcendent standard.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Fallible access is plainly compatible with objective truth, and selfishness coherently explains some failures without implying relativism.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual distinction is strong, while selfishness as a broad explanation of social error receives limited representative support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary theistic disagreement-and-application bridge near the top of that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move handles the disagreement objection fairly, with a bounded omission concerning the secular realist's equal access to the distinction.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes moral epistemology from ontology and says objective values need not be easy or infallibly grasped by selfish humans.

moves.speaker: Shelly Kagan
moves.proposition: Secular moral realism can explain widespread historical error as gradual discovery through reasoning that corrects inherited tendencies.
moves.attributionBasis: Kagan explicitly agrees with much of Craig's diagnosis, then supplies an evolutionary and rational account of progress toward recognition of moral truths.

components.text: Explain on secular premises how widespread historical moral error can coexist with objective truth and subsequent moral progress.

response.rationale: The move accepts fallibility and offers gradual reflective discovery, including correction of inherited evolutionary tendencies, as a secular progress mechanism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it directly contacts the compatibility demand but gives only a compressed account of reliability and correction.

precisionFindings.rationale: Gradual discovery is clear, but the mechanisms by which reasoning reliably corrects inherited tendencies are only broadly specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The analogy with discovery in other domains makes progress plausible but does not fully establish the reliability of moral reflection.

charity.alternative: Fallibility may be compatible with truth while still leaving secular moral inquiry without a uniquely reliable correction method.
charity.decisiveQualification: General intellectual progress does not automatically establish convergence on objective moral facts.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The compatibility account is coherent, with one material bridge from reflective reasoning to reliable identification of moral truth.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The cross-domain analogy and evolutionary story are relevant, though representative evidence of the correction mechanism is limited.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly completes a major supporting step in the subsidiary secular error-and-progress bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly accepts the epistemic problem but compresses the strongest reliability qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt compares moral discovery with gradual discovery in other domains and invokes reasoning as a correction to inherited tendencies.

moves.speaker: Shelly Kagan
moves.proposition: Finite loving relationships and moral actions can possess genuine objective value despite eventual death and cosmic extinction.
moves.attributionBasis: Kagan identifies the essential disagreement with Craig and develops a continuous closing argument using finite loving relationships as his central counterexample.

components.text: Identify why lack of eternal cosmic significance does not entail lack of genuine objective value in finite relationships and actions.

response.rationale: The move explicitly rejects the permanence-to-value inference and supplies loving relationships as a counterexample whose reality and value do not depend on eternity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it names the exact inference under dispute and directly provides a counterexample to it.

precisionFindings.rationale: Eternal cosmic significance and genuine objective value are explicitly distinguished, and the finite-love example has clear scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The example adequately defeats the alleged entailment without claiming to prove every component of secular moral realism.

charity.alternative: The opponent may reserve 'ultimate significance' for value that survives extinction rather than deny all finite value.
charity.decisiveQualification: That stipulated category cannot establish that finite love lacks genuine objective value during or because of its finitude.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction and counterexample directly block the inference from impermanence to valuelessness with no substantial internal tension.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A loving relationship is a specific and representative counterexample, though its objective status remains a basic realist commitment.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central finite-significance bridge by grounding genuine value in finite relationships and actions.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response preserves the narrower eternal-significance claim while accurately rejecting its extension to all objective value.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly calls the inference from no eternal cosmic significance to no objective significance mistaken and cites finite love as genuinely valuable.
